candidates.note: marginal: formative-years fan, nothing explicit about his own music

candidates.speaker: Richard H. Kirk of Cabaret Voltaire
candidates.sentence: I was a Bowie fan from about 15. I went to see the Ziggy Stardust tour in Sheffield and was kind of blown away as much by the way he looked.
candidates.citation: Richard H. Kirk of Cabaret Voltaire, choosing David Bowie's Low for The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "I was a Bowie fan from about 15."
candidates.note: marginal: fan in formative years; Low itself is described as a turning point for electronic music

candidates.speaker: Steve Diggle of Buzzcocks
candidates.sentence: Bowie was an inspiration to [Buzzcocks] like The Beatles were.
candidates.citation: Steve Diggle of Buzzcocks, choosing David Bowie's 'Panic In Detroit' for The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "Bowie was an inspiration to [Buzzcocks] like The Beatles were."

candidates.speaker: Stuart Murdoch of Belle and Sebastian
candidates.sentence: The Smiths were playing ‘Bigmouth Strikes Again’, and during the course of that song I became a different person.
candidates.citation: Stuart Murdoch of Belle and Sebastian, choosing The Smiths's The Queen Is Dead for The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "during the course of that song I became a different person."

candidates.speaker: Stuart Murdoch of Belle and Sebastian
candidates.sentence: It had a great effect on me at the time, but I don’t listen to The Fall very often now. It went along with my abrasive nature at the time – this crazy ranter, Mark E Smith, appealed to me deeply.
candidates.citation: Stuart Murdoch of Belle and Sebastian, choosing The Fall's This Nation's Saving Grace for The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "It had a great effect on me at the time, but I don't listen to The Fall very often now."
candidates.note: marginal: effect on him as a young listener, not on his songwriting

candidates.speaker: Johnny Marr of The Smiths
candidates.sentence: As a young guitar player, discovering 154 showed me a world that was an alternative way of looking at the instrument. It has stuck with me all the way through my career.
candidates.citation: Johnny Marr of The Smiths, choosing Wire's 154 for The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "As a young guitar player, discovering 154 showed me a world that was an alternative way of looking at the instrument. It has stuck with me all the way through my career."

candidates.speaker: Johnny Marr of The Smiths
candidates.sentence: Buzzcocks influenced The Smiths massively in the way we approached our record sleeves and our choice of independent record company – because of the Buzzcocks we took on a Mancunian DIY ethic, whilst being in the charts.
candidates.citation: Johnny Marr of The Smiths, choosing Buzzcocks's Another Music In A Different Kitchen for The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "Buzzcocks influenced The Smiths massively in the way we approached our record sleeves and our choice of independent record company"

candidates.speaker: Johnny Marr of The Smiths
candidates.sentence: with me being a teenager during the 70s meant I never stopped being affected by Brian’s music.
candidates.citation: Johnny Marr of The Smiths, choosing Brian Eno's Taking Tiger Mountain (By Strategy) for The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "with me being a teenager during the 70s meant I never stopped being affected by Brian's music"
candidates.note: marginal: general effect of Eno's music on him as a teenager; the Taking Tiger Mountain remarks are about the record's reach

candidates.speaker: Dan Snaith of Caribou
candidates.sentence: People who know my albums from ten years ago will have heard me trying to rip off Silver Apples.
candidates.citation: Dan Snaith of Caribou, choosing Silver Apples' debut for The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "People who know my albums from ten years ago will have heard me trying to rip off Silver Apples."

candidates.speaker: Michelle Zauner of Japanese Breakfast
candidates.sentence: When I started playing guitar, it was important for me to learn how to do finger-picking style because of those Elliott Smith records.
candidates.citation: Michelle Zauner of Japanese Breakfast, choosing Elliott Smith's XO for The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "When I started playing guitar, it was important for me to learn how to do finger-picking style because of those Elliott Smith records."

candidates.speaker: Michelle Zauner of Japanese Breakfast
candidates.sentence: Musicians like her and Kimya Dawson had these very singular voices that were great for me. I loved their songwriting and the character in it and sort of gave me the courage to be a singer without sounding like Aretha Franklin or something.
candidates.citation: Michelle Zauner of Japanese Breakfast, choosing Joanna Newsom's Ys for The Quietus's Baker's Dozen, said Newsom's songwriting "sort of gave me the courage to be a singer without sounding like Aretha Franklin or something."

candidates.speaker: Michelle Zauner of Japanese Breakfast
candidates.sentence: My other big influence on [For Melancholy Brunettes (& Sad Women)] was Sufjan Stevens’ Carrie & Lowell.
candidates.citation: Michelle Zauner of Japanese Breakfast, choosing Sufjan Stevens' Carrie & Lowell for The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "My other big influence on [For Melancholy Brunettes (& Sad Women)] was Sufjan Stevens' Carrie & Lowell."

candidates.speaker: Lol Tolhurst of The Cure
candidates.sentence: I’ve actually got part of a chapter in my new book about how Joe Strummer started me on this path.
candidates.citation: Lol Tolhurst of The Cure, choosing The Clash's debut for The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "I've actually got part of a chapter in my new book about how Joe Strummer started me on this path."

candidates.speaker: Lol Tolhurst of The Cure
candidates.sentence: What I always thought of with the drums was once the rhythm’s there, there’s this whole space inside of it that you can listen to and focus on with the push and pull. That’s what I was always trying for.
candidates.citation: Lol Tolhurst of The Cure, choosing Can's Tago Mago for The Quietus's Baker's Dozen, on Jaki Liebezeit's drumming: "there's this whole space inside of it that you can listen to and focus on with the push and pull. That's what I was always trying for."
candidates.note: Moderate: about drumming approach rather than the record itself; he also names Can alongside Cluster in his Low pick.

candidates.speaker: Joey Santiago of Pixies
candidates.sentence: That probably seeped in to [his and Black Francis’ playing] on ‘Monkey Gone To Heaven’ through osmosis.
candidates.citation: Joey Santiago of Pixies, choosing Television's Marquee Moon for The Quietus's Baker's Dozen, said its trading of rhythm and lead "probably seeped in" to his and Black Francis's playing on "Monkey Gone To Heaven" "through osmosis".
candidates.note: Hedged ('probably', 'we didn't mean it'); Marquee Moon was heard after Pixies had started. Owner may prefer favourite.

candidates.speaker: Mike Watt of Minutemen
candidates.sentence: When D’s mom makes us into a band and puts me on bass (I bought my first bass for $100), I had to learn bass from Fun House, Creedence and the brothers doing R&B, or like Trevor Bolder [of Bowie’s Spider From Mars and Uriah Heep], because you could really hear the bass on British rock & roll – most US rock & roll buried the bass in the mix.
candidates.citation: Mike Watt of Minutemen, choosing The Stooges' Fun House for The Quietus's Baker's Dozen, said that when he was put on bass, "I had to learn bass from Fun House, Creedence and the brothers doing R&B", and that Fun House was "a freak out moment for us" and "the lingua franca" of their scene.

candidates.speaker: Will Sergeant of Echo & the Bunnymen
candidates.sentence: I learnt all the wobbly guitar sounds you hear on the Bunnymen records from this. I’ve been living off that ever since, really.
candidates.citation: Will Sergeant of Echo & the Bunnymen, choosing Television's Marquee Moon for The Quietus's Baker's Dozen: "I learnt all the wobbly guitar sounds you hear on the Bunnymen records from this. I've been living off that ever since, really."

candidates.speaker: Will Sergeant of Echo & the Bunnymen
candidates.sentence: And I thought, ‘right, I can kinda do that!’ And that’s when I started getting into recording, buying tape recorders and equipment, because I saw myself more as a creator than a guitarist.
candidates.citation: Will Sergeant of Echo & the Bunnymen, choosing Brian Eno's Another Green World for The Quietus's Baker's Dozen, on watching Eno with Roxy Music: "I thought, 'right, I can kinda do that!' And that's when I started getting into recording, buying tape recorders and equipment".

candidates.speaker: Alan Sparhawk of Low
candidates.sentence: I remember learning the chords to that song on the guitar, and that was the big lightning bolt going on.
candidates.citation: Alan Sparhawk of Low, choosing The Clash's Combat Rock for The Quietus's Baker's Dozen, on learning "Should I Stay Or Should I Go?": "I remember learning the chords to that song on the guitar, and that was the big lightning bolt going on."
